title: Law doesn't guarantee that any particular constituency be reserved for SC/STs: Supreme Court

 Litigation News Law doesn't guarantee that any particular constituency be reserved for SC/STs: Supreme Court 
 The Court observed that the law guarantees proportionate reservation based on SC/ST population, but does not guarantee reservation of any particular constituency. Supreme Court of India Debayan Roy Published on :  16 Nov 2026, 7:37 am 2 min read 
 Copied 
 Follow Us Listen to this article The Supreme Court on Monday held that no voter or candidate has a vested right to have a particular constituency reserved for Scheduled Castes (SC) or Scheduled Tribe (ST) candidates [ Sau Rupali Indrabhusam Sonde v. State of Maharashtra & Ors] .
 A Bench of Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana made the observation while dismissing a plea challenging the manner of rotation of seats reserved for SCs and STs in Maharashtra's zilla parishad and panchayat samiti elections.
 The Court rejected the argument that Rule 12 of the Maharashtra Zilla Parishads and Panchayat Samitis (Manner and Rotation of Reservation of Seats) Rules, 2025, which resets the reference point for rotation of reserved constituencies, makes the very concept of rotation illusory.
 Justice Bagchi observed that while the law provides for rotation of reserved seats in descending order of the SC/ST population in constituencies, the manner and timeframe for carrying out such rotation are within the government's discretion.
 "We have considered the submissions advanced that Rule 12 having shifted the cut-off date for rotation of constituencies for the purposes of reservation, makes the very concept of rotation illusory. Though the argument is attractive at first blush, the same fails to take into consideration that no voter or candidate can have a vested right to have a particular constituency reserved," the Court said.
 Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana The Court held that under Rule 12, the next general election after the 2025 amendment will be treated as the starting point for the rotation of reserved seats.
 "We find no reason to hold that the said rule runs counter to either the concept of reservation or rotation of seats," the Court held before dismissing the plea.
 The plea was filed by one Rupali Indrabhushan Sonde after the Bombay High Court's Nagpur Bench dismissed her challenge to Rule 12 in September 2025.
 The provision is part of the Maharashtra Zilla Parishads and Panchayat Samitis (Manner and Rotation of Reservation of Seats) Rules, 2025, which replaced the earlier 1996 rules. It provides for reservation of seats in zilla parishads in proportion to the SC/ST population in the respective areas.
 The petitioners had argued before the High Court that the introduction of this provision disrupted the existing rotation cycle and could prevent several candidates from contesting elections from reserved constituencies.
 Th plea also contended that the rule was arbitrary and violated Article 14 of the Constitution, which guarantees equality before the law
 During the Supreme Court hearing, counsel for the petitioner argued that repeatedly resetting the rotation cycle could effectively prevent constituencies with smaller SC/ST populations from ever being reserved.
 However, the Supreme Court rejected this argument. It held that the law guarantees proportionate reservation and rotation of seats, but does not guarantee that any particular constituency will be reserved.
 On November 4, the top court had dismissed a petition challenging the continued reservation of certain assembly constituencies for SC/ST candidates without rotation for several decades.
